## Summary

  PR #2253 establishes one central rule:

  > Checkpoint IDs found anywhere in a commit message may be used for historical discovery, but only IDs in Git’s final trailer block may authorize checkpoint creation, reuse, reconciliation, or
  > mutation.

  Previously, a body paragraph containing Entire-Checkpoint: <existing-id> could redirect operations toward an unrelated checkpoint. That affected PostCommit condensation, attach, generated
  explanations, and legacy session reconciliation.

  There are no new CLI commands, flags, or storage formats. This is a parsing and authorization-boundary change.

  A concrete example:

  Implement feature

  Entire-Checkpoint: A

  Additional body text

  Signed-off-by: Developer <dev@example.com>

  - Read-only historical discovery still finds A, preserving squash-merge history.
  - Mutation paths do not accept A, because the final trailer block contains only Signed-off-by.

  If the message instead ends with:

  Signed-off-by: Developer <dev@example.com>
  Entire-Checkpoint: B

  then B is the mutation-authorizing checkpoint.

  ## Semantic changes

   Area                         Before                                                                            After
  ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━  ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━  ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
   Checkpoint parsing           One permissive parser searched the whole message                                  Separate discovery and mutation parsers
  ───────────────────────────  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   PostCommit                   Body text could select the condensation target                                    Only a final-block checkpoint triggers condensation
  ───────────────────────────  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   Attach                       Body text could select an existing checkpoint and receive the attached session    Attach reuses only a final-block ID; otherwise it creates a fresh checkpoint
  ───────────────────────────  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   Commit preparation           Body text could suppress stamping a real trailer                                  A fresh final trailer is added unless one genuinely exists
  ───────────────────────────  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   Amend                        Body text could be mistaken for an existing trailer                               Only an effective final trailer is preserved
  ───────────────────────────  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   Explain generation           --generate could write a summary to a body-selected checkpoint                    Generation requires final-block authority
  ───────────────────────────  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   Read-only explain/history    Could discover embedded squash trailers                                           Unchanged
  ───────────────────────────  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   Legacy migration             A matching body ID could realign attribution state                                Reconciliation requires a final-block match
  ───────────────────────────  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   Trailer grammar              Indented pseudo-trailers were accepted                                            Leading whitespace disqualifies them as trailers
  ───────────────────────────  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   Continuations                Multiline Git trailers could invalidate the block                                 Indented lines after a real trailer are accepted as continuations
  ───────────────────────────  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   Commit comments              Assumed # and stripped it indiscriminately                                        Follows core.commentString, core.commentChar, and auto, with source-aware cleanup

  ## Why the parser was split instead of globally tightened

  The checkpoint transcripts record that making ParseCheckpoint globally strict was deliberately rejected.

  Squash merges commonly embed original commit messages like this:

  Squashed commit:

  First change

  Entire-Checkpoint: A

  Second change

  Entire-Checkpoint: B

  Those checkpoint lines are body paragraphs in the resulting squash commit. Resume and read-only history discovery need to find both.

  Unfortunately, a legitimate embedded squash trailer and malicious checkpoint-shaped body text can be byte-for-byte identical. Looking up whether the checkpoint exists does not authenticate it—an
  attacker can name an existing ID.

  Therefore the implementation uses two levels of evidence:

  - Whole-message occurrence: sufficient for discovery.
  - Final-trailer-block placement: sufficient for local mutation decisions.

  “Final-block authority” is intentionally not described as cryptographic trust; a user can still deliberately author a final trailer.

  ## File-by-file explanation

  ### Production changes

  1. cmd/entire/cli/trailers/trailers.go:152

  Introduces:

  - ParseCheckpointFromFinalTrailerBlock
  - ParseAllCheckpointsFromFinalTrailerBlock

  The existing ParseCheckpoint and ParseAllCheckpoints remain permissive, but their contracts now explicitly describe their results as discovery candidates rather than mutation authority.

  The strict parser:

  - Inspects only the last non-empty paragraph.
  - Requires unindented Key: value lines.
  - Allows whitespace-leading continuation lines only after a genuine trailer.
  - Never interprets a continuation as a new checkpoint.
  - Validates checkpoint IDs.
  - Deduplicates multiple IDs while preserving order.
  - Returns the first ID from the singular API.

  finalTrailerBlock was also corrected not to TrimSpace before classifying a line. Otherwise:

    Entire-Checkpoint: A

  would incorrectly become a valid trailer even though Git treats it as body/continuation text.

  HasOPFApplied now follows the same unindented semantics, preventing an indented Entire-OPF-Applied: true from being accepted.

  2. cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_hooks.go:145

  All commit lifecycle mutation decisions move to final-block parsing:

  - PrepareCommitMsg no longer lets a body ID suppress creation of the session’s real checkpoint trailer.
  - handleAmendCommitMsg preserves only a genuine final trailer; otherwise it may restore the session’s recorded ID.
  - The agent-commit fast path applies the same rule.
  - CommitMsg checks only the effective final trailer before deciding whether an otherwise empty commit should have Entire’s trailer removed.
  - PostCommit condenses session data only when HEAD has a final-block checkpoint.

  The file also gains source-aware commit-message cleanup:

  - Editor/template flows remove lines Git will treat as comments before locating the final trailer block.
  - -m and -F flows preserve comment-prefixed lines because they are user-supplied content, not editor boilerplate.

  That distinction prevents this -m message from being misread:

  Subject

  Entire-Checkpoint: A
  # actual user content

  Stripping # actual user content would falsely promote A into the final block.

  Comment handling now reads Git configuration in this precedence order:

  1. core.commentString
  2. core.commentChar
  3. Default #

  For auto, it chooses the first candidate not already starting a message line. Entire’s explanatory comments are emitted using that same prefix.

  CommitMsg strips comments for validation only when Entire’s own “Remove the Entire-Checkpoint…” marker is present. That avoids treating arbitrary user-authored comment-looking lines as disposable.

  3. cmd/entire/cli/attach.go:651

  Two decisions are hardened:

  - resolveCheckpointID reuses only IDs from HEAD’s final trailer block.
  - promptAmendCommit considers a checkpoint already attached only if that exact ID is in the final block.

  Consequently, a body reference cannot make attach append a transcript to an unrelated existing checkpoint or avoid adding the real trailer.

  When several final checkpoint trailers exist, attach preserves the previous policy of selecting the last one.

  4. cmd/entire/cli/explain.go:3012

  Adds parseCheckpointForExplainCommit, which chooses parsing policy according to the operation:

  - Read-only explanation uses whole-message discovery.
  - --generate uses final-block parsing because it eventually calls store.Write.

  This is applied to both:

  - Explicit checkpoint explain --commit <ref>
  - Positional target resolution that falls back from checkpoint lookup to a commit

  This preserves squash-history explanation while stopping generated summaries from being written to a checkpoint named only in commit-body text.

  5. cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_migration.go:33

  Legacy states may lack LastCheckpointCommitHash. Previously, a whole-message match against LastCheckpointID could select the reconciliation path and realign both BaseCommit and
  AttributionBaseCommit.

  Now the ID must appear in the final trailer block. A body-only match falls through to ordinary migration, leaving the attribution base pinned.

  The recorded rationale is that backward compatibility should not allow weaker evidence to mutate future attribution.

  ### Test changes

  6. cmd/entire/cli/trailers/trailers_test.go:346

  Covers the parser contract:

  - Body checkpoint followed by a different final block
  - Final versus embedded IDs
  - Multiple and duplicate final IDs
  - Checkpoint text inside another trailer’s value
  - Space- and tab-indented pseudo-trailers
  - Valid continuation lines
  - A continuation containing checkpoint-shaped text
  - Singular parser returning the first final ID

  It also adds t.Parallel() to the existing checkpoint parser test; that has no product semantic effect.

  7. cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_test.go:872

  Updates existing helper calls for the new comment-prefix parameter and verifies:

  - Custom core.commentChar
  - core.commentString precedence
  - auto avoiding an already-used prefix
  - Editor comments being cleaned
  - -m/-F comment-looking user content being preserved
  - Entire’s explanatory comments using the configured prefix

  8. cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_worktree_session_test.go:46

  Extracts shared setup and adds a hook-level regression:

  - Input contains forged checkpoint-shaped body text.
  - PrepareCommitMsg stamps a new final checkpoint.
  - Whole-message discovery still returns both IDs.

  This directly demonstrates the discovery/authorization split.

  9. cmd/entire/cli/strategy/phase_postcommit_test.go:75

  Proves an indented pseudo-trailer does not authorize condensation:

  - Session StepCount remains unchanged.
  - No persistent checkpoint branch is created.

  10. cmd/entire/cli/attach_test.go:2021

  Exercises the durable attach boundary rather than just parser helpers:

  - Creates an existing checkpoint containing an unrelated session.
  - Creates HEAD with either a body checkpoint or indented pseudo-trailer naming that checkpoint.
  - Runs real attach logic.
  - Verifies the unrelated checkpoint remains untouched.
  - Verifies the attached transcript is written under a newly generated checkpoint.

  11. cmd/entire/cli/explain_test.go:445

  Verifies both explicit and positional --generate paths reject a body-selected ID, while a separate test confirms read-only explain still discovers it.

  12. cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_migration_test.go:212

  Creates legacy state without LastCheckpointCommitHash and a commit containing:

  - The session’s ID in the body
  - A different ID in the final trailer block

  It verifies normal migration occurs and AttributionBaseCommit is not realigned.

  ## How the two commits evolved

  - 2d16b3666 introduced the discovery-versus-mutation parser split and applied it to hooks and attach.
  - ba2a0d923 completed the boundary after review found four gaps:
      - Explain generation
      - Legacy migration
      - Indented pseudo-trailers
      - Incorrect hard-coded comment cleanup

  The second commit also added Git-style continuation support and upgraded attach testing to inspect persistent storage.

  One review concern—hasUserContent treating checkpoint-shaped-only content specially—was dismissed because that behavior predates this branch and is not a regression introduced here.

  ## Current branch and PR state

  - HEAD: ba2a0d923
  - Two commits over the merge base fce049cd3
  - Diff: 12 files, 530 additions, 43 deletions
  - Local-only untracked files: progress.md and review.md
  - Local main is behind upstream/main, but both three-dot comparisons produce the same 12-file PR change set.
  - The PR is currently a mergeable draft, blocked from merging by draft/review state. No GitHub reviews or comments are currently recorded.
  - GitHub currently reports a neutral Entire Gates check.

  The PR records successful lint, unit, integration, CI canary, and diff-check runs. Checkpoint history confirms no paid real-agent E2E was run. During this read-only analysis I independently reran
  only git diff --check, which passed.

Entire Replay:

Replaying: checkpoint final-trailer mutation boundary  
Total steps: 2  
Date range: 2026-09-02 11:07 → 17:07  
Primary author: Muskan Paliwal

## Step 1 of 2 · Sep 2 · Initial boundary fix

The first step was identifying that **checkpoint discovery and checkpoint authority are different jobs**.

**Why this happened:** The old parser searched the entire commit message. Consequently, checkpoint-shaped body text could redirect a write operation toward an existing checkpoint.

Consider:

```text
Implement feature

Entire-Checkpoint: A

Additional explanation

Signed-off-by: Developer <dev@example.com>
```

The final trailer block is only:

```text
Signed-off-by: Developer <dev@example.com>
```

So `A` is useful historical evidence, but it should not authorize modifying checkpoint `A`.

**The tempting fix:** Make the existing parser inspect only the final trailer block.

That would stop the attack—but break squash history:

```text
Squashed changes

First commit

Entire-Checkpoint: A

Second commit

Entire-Checkpoint: B
```

After a squash, both checkpoint lines are embedded body paragraphs. Resume needs to discover both and choose the latest valid checkpoint.

**The key decision:** Split parsing into two levels of evidence:

```text
Whole-message occurrence ──► historical discovery
Final trailer block ───────► creation, reuse, or mutation
```

An analogy: finding someone’s address in an old document can help you locate them, but it is not authorization to access their account.

Quick understanding check: in the first example, should read-only history find `A`, should mutation accept `A`, or both?

Ready for step 2? (Or ask a question about this step.)
what is the issue?. help me understand in simple terms. like why is this a bug?

The bug is that Entire treated **checkpoint-looking text anywhere in a commit message as real instructions**.

A checkpoint ID points to stored agent-session data. Imagine checkpoint `A` belongs to an older, unrelated session.

Someone writes this commit:

```text
Fix login bug

While investigating, I found this old reference:

Entire-Checkpoint: A

More explanation follows.
```

That `Entire-Checkpoint: A` is plainly part of the description. But the old parser searched the whole message, found `A`, and effectively concluded:

> “This commit is officially connected to checkpoint A.”

That conclusion could affect write operations. Entire might:

- append the current session to checkpoint `A`;
- condense or update checkpoint `A`;
- avoid creating the correct new checkpoint;
- associate the wrong transcript with the commit.

So harmless-looking body text could redirect Entire toward unrelated stored data.

A simple analogy: suppose an email says:

```text
Please investigate invoice #123.

For reference, the old account number was:
Destination-Account: 999

Thanks
```

A payment system should not transfer money to account `999` merely because that text appeared somewhere in the email. It needs a clearly designated instruction field.

Git has such a designated area: the **final trailer block**, at the bottom of the commit:

```text
Fix login bug

More explanation.

Signed-off-by: Developer <dev@example.com>
Entire-Checkpoint: B
```

Here, `B` is deliberately placed among the commit’s final metadata trailers, so mutation operations may use it.

The core bug was therefore:

```text
mentioned somewhere = authorized instruction
```

Those are not equivalent.

The fix changes the rule to:

```text
Mentioned anywhere       → may help find historical information
Placed in final trailers → may authorize checkpoint writes or reuse
```

This matters even without a malicious attacker. An old checkpoint line copied into documentation, a squash-merged commit, or an example in the message could accidentally cause Entire to modify the wrong checkpoint.

Quick check: in this message, should `A` authorize a checkpoint update?

```text
Fix parser

Example of the previous output:
Entire-Checkpoint: A

Reviewed-by: Sam <sam@example.com>
```

Answer: no. `A` is body content; the final trailer block contains only `Reviewed-by`.

Ready for step 2? (Or another question.)
what does authorise checkpoint update mean?

Here, “authorize” does **not** mean cryptographic permission or user authentication.

It means:

> “Does Entire have enough evidence to treat this checkpoint ID as the intended target of a write operation?”

A checkpoint is stored data connected to an agent session—for example, its transcript and metadata. Suppose checkpoint `A` already contains Alice’s earlier session.

Now you run an operation that needs to save your current session. Entire must decide:

```text
Update existing checkpoint A?
            or
Create a new checkpoint B?
```

If the commit merely mentions `A` in its body, that is not enough evidence to choose the first option. Otherwise, Entire could mix your new session into unrelated checkpoint `A`.

“Checkpoint update” covers actions such as:

- attaching another session transcript to an existing checkpoint;
- condensing or finalizing session data under that checkpoint;
- generating and saving an explanation for it;
- reconciling legacy session state around it;
- reusing the checkpoint instead of creating a fresh one.

For example:

```text
Fix authentication

This reproduces a problem originally seen in:
Entire-Checkpoint: A

More details...
```

The old behavior could interpret that as:

```text
Write the current session’s data into A
```

The corrected behavior interprets it as:

```text
A is mentioned historically.
Do not write to A.
Create a fresh checkpoint instead.
```

But if the message ends with:

```text
Fix authentication

More details...

Entire-Checkpoint: A
```

then Entire’s policy says the final trailer is strong enough evidence that `A` was intentionally selected.

So “authorization” here means **authorization within the program’s decision rules**, not secure proof of identity. A user can deliberately type a final trailer themselves.

The simplest distinction is:

```text
Reading:
“Which checkpoints does this commit mention?”

Writing:
“Which checkpoint did this commit deliberately designate?”
```

Ready for step 2? (Or another question.)

But there is one subtle lesson already: even “resume” changes local state, so calling it merely read-only would be too loose. Yes. The original bug is an implicit assumption:

> “Text that looks like metadata was intentionally supplied as metadata.”

That assumption becomes dangerous only when the result controls a consequential action.

I did a targeted graph-backed audit of the Go code. Most remaining whole-message checkpoint parsing is used only for discovery, attribution, status, review context, and dispatch. Those uses appear consistent with the new contract. But I found several assumptions worth investigating.

| Assumption | Where | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Trailer writer and reader recognize the same grammar | [trailers.go](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/fix-checkpoint-trailer-block/cmd/entire/cli/trailers/trailers.go:241) | Likely bug |
| Multiple final checkpoint trailers have one clear winner | [trailers.go](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/fix-checkpoint-trailer-block/cmd/entire/cli/trailers/trailers.go:150), [attach.go](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/fix-checkpoint-trailer-block/cmd/entire/cli/attach.go:651) | Inconsistent policy |
| An existing body-mentioned checkpoint is suitable for explicit resume | [checkpoint_resume.go](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/fix-checkpoint-trailer-block/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint_resume.go:187) | Deliberate residual risk |
| Shadow-branch commit messages are inherently trustworthy | [trailers.go](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/fix-checkpoint-trailer-block/cmd/entire/cli/trailers/trailers.go:75), [ephemeral.go](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/fix-checkpoint-trailer-block/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/ephemeral.go:209) | Needs boundary review |
| “Latest checkpoint” means greatest stored `CreatedAt` | [manual_commit_pending.go](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/fix-checkpoint-trailer-block/cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_pending.go:290) | Explicit but important assumption |

The strongest new candidate is a writer–reader disagreement.

The writer trims leading whitespace when deciding whether a paragraph is already a trailer block:

```go
last := strings.TrimSpace(lines[i])
if IsTrailerLine(last) {
    // treat as a trailer block
}
```

But the strict reader correctly does not trim leading whitespace.

Given:

```text
Subject

  Entire-Checkpoint: A
```

the writer may append `B` without inserting a separating blank line:

```text
Subject

  Entire-Checkpoint: A
Entire-Checkpoint: B
```

The strict reader then rejects the entire paragraph because its first line is indented. Entire appears to have added `B`, but later mutation paths cannot recognize it. That looks like a genuine correctness gap; it is inferred from current code and does not appear covered by the existing tests.

There is also a multiple-trailer disagreement:

```text
Entire-Checkpoint: A
Entire-Checkpoint: B
```

- The singular strict parser returns the first: `A`.
- Attach deliberately selects the last: `B`.

Therefore PostCommit/explain generation and attach can interpret the same final block differently. Entire normally produces one checkpoint trailer, so this is an edge case, but ambiguity should probably be rejected or resolved centrally.

The replay’s recorded intent explicitly accepts another assumption for compatibility: body IDs may be resume candidates if corresponding checkpoint data exists. Existence does not authenticate the association—someone can name a real checkpoint—but `entire checkpoint resume <commit>` is an explicit user operation that reads that checkpoint and restores local state. That is a conscious trade-off, not an unnoticed parser mistake.

Finally, `ParseSession`, `ParseMetadata`, and `ParseTaskMetadata` still search anywhere and return the first occurrence. Their callers assume ephemeral shadow commits were generated by Entire. That assumption deserves examination because the leading commit text originates from a cleaned user prompt and could contain trailer-shaped text.

So yes: this PR fixes one instance of a broader recurring pattern:

```text
Recognizable syntax
        ↓
Assumed provenance or intent
        ↓
Consequential behavior
```

The next useful investigation would be the writer–reader mismatch first; it is the most concrete newly identified gap. No files were changed during this audit.

content.text:
## Step 2 of 2 · Sep 2 · Closing the remaining gaps

The first commit established the rule, but review found that the rule was not yet enforced everywhere.

**What changed since the last step:** The initial fix protected commit hooks and attach. The second step audited other operations that could write or realign checkpoint data.

Four gaps were found:

1. **Explain generation**

Read-only explain may discover a checkpoint from body text. But `--generate` saves a generated summary, so it must require a final trailer.

```text
Body mentions A
Final trailers contain B

Read explanation → may discover A
Generate summary → may write only to B
```

2. **Legacy migration**

Migration can change attribution state. It previously allowed a body occurrence to prove that an old session belonged to a checkpoint. That evidence was too weak for changing future attribution.

3. **Git trailer grammar**

This is not a real trailer:

```text
  Entire-Checkpoint: A
```

Leading whitespace makes it body or continuation text. However, indentation is valid after a real trailer:

```text
Notes: Long explanation
 continuation of the explanation
Entire-Checkpoint: B
```

The parser therefore needed to distinguish a continuation from a new trailer.

4. **Commit comments**

Editor-created messages contain disposable comment lines:

```text
# Please enter the commit message...
```

But `#` can also be deliberate user content when supplied through `git commit -m` or `-F`.

That distinction matters here:

```text
Subject

Entire-Checkpoint: A
# actual user content
```

If Entire always deleted `# actual user content`, it would accidentally make `A` look like the final trailer block. The fix therefore considers both the Git-configured comment prefix and how the message was supplied.

The deeper lesson was:

> Defining a security boundary is insufficient; every operation that crosses it must use the correct parser and the correct preprocessing.

## Journey takeaways

- Discovery evidence and mutation authority require separate APIs.
- Valid syntax does not prove provenance, intent, or permission.
- A safety rule must be applied at the final write decision—not only in a shared parser.
- Preprocessing can silently change security meaning.
- Tests should exercise durable effects, such as which checkpoint was actually written, rather than only parser output.

what is a trailer and I'm not getting anything. Can you just make me understand in simple terms like the problem and the solution that we came up with?

Let’s reset and explain it from scratch.

## What is a trailer?

A Git commit has a message:

```text
Fix the login page
```

It can also have extra information at the bottom:

```text
Fix the login page

Signed-off-by: Muskan <muskan@example.com>
Entire-Checkpoint: ABC123
```

Those bottom `Name: value` lines are called **trailers**.

Think of them as labeled fields on a form:

```text
Author: Muskan
Checkpoint: ABC123
```

Entire uses this trailer:

```text
Entire-Checkpoint: ABC123
```

It means:

> “This commit is connected to checkpoint ABC123.”

A checkpoint stores information from an agent session, such as its transcript and metadata.

## What was the bug?

Entire looked for `Entire-Checkpoint:` **anywhere** in the commit message.

Consider this commit:

```text
Fix the login page

This bug was previously discussed in:

Entire-Checkpoint: OLD123

More explanation follows.
```

Here, `OLD123` is only mentioned in the description. It is not an official metadata field at the bottom.

But Entire saw the matching text and thought:

> “This commit wants to use checkpoint OLD123.”

Entire could then put new session information into the old, unrelated checkpoint.

The mistake was:

```text
“This text mentions OLD123”
```

being treated as:

```text
“Please update OLD123”
```

Those mean different things.

## What solution did we choose?

Entire now asks two different questions.

### Question 1: Does the message mention a checkpoint?

For searching old history, Entire checks the whole message:

```text
Entire-Checkpoint: OLD123
```

Even if it appears in the middle, Entire may use it to help find historical information.

### Question 2: Which checkpoint should Entire update?

For writing data, Entire accepts only a checkpoint trailer in the final metadata section:

```text
Fix the login page

Some explanation.

Signed-off-by: Muskan <muskan@example.com>
Entire-Checkpoint: NEW456
```

Because `NEW456` is in the bottom trailer section, Entire treats it as the intended checkpoint.

So the new rule is:

```text
Mentioned in the message
        ↓
Useful for searching history

Placed in the final trailer section
        ↓
May be used for writing checkpoint data
```

## Why not ignore every checkpoint in the body?

Because squash merges combine several commits into one:

```text
Combined changes

First original commit
Entire-Checkpoint: AAA111

Second original commit
Entire-Checkpoint: BBB222
```

Those checkpoint lines are now in the body, but they remain useful historical information. Entire needs them to find the sessions behind the original commits.

Therefore, we cannot simply say:

> “Body checkpoint lines are always useless.”

Instead, we say:

> “Body checkpoint lines are useful for searching, but not powerful enough to select where new data is written.”

## Simple analogy

Imagine this delivery form:

```text
Notes:
My previous address was 10 Old Street.

Deliver to:
25 New Street
```

Searching the document should find both addresses.

But the delivery driver should deliver only to the address in the official **Deliver to** field.

For Entire:

```text
Commit body        = Notes
Final trailer block = Deliver to
```

That is the entire problem and solution:

> Entire previously confused a mention with an instruction. Now it keeps mentions for history but requires an official bottom trailer before writing to a checkpoint.
and how do we know if it's a sqaush merge?

We generally **cannot reliably know** that a commit is a squash merge.

A squash commit might look like:

```text
Combine login changes

First change
Entire-Checkpoint: AAA111

Second change
Entire-Checkpoint: BBB222
```

But a person could manually write exactly the same message:

```text
Combine login changes

First change
Entire-Checkpoint: AAA111

Second change
Entire-Checkpoint: BBB222
```

After the commit exists, those messages are identical. Git does not attach a trustworthy flag saying:

```text
This commit was created by a squash merge.
```

We could guess based on wording such as “Squashed commit,” but wording is customizable and easy to imitate. That would not be a safe rule.

So the solution deliberately avoids asking:

> “Is this a squash merge?”

Instead, it asks:

> “What is Entire about to do with the checkpoint ID?”

- If Entire is only searching history, checkpoint IDs anywhere in the message are accepted as **possible historical references**.
- If Entire is about to write or modify checkpoint data, only an ID in the final trailer section is accepted.

In short:

```text
We cannot reliably identify squash commits.

Therefore:

Body checkpoint → possible historical clue
Final trailer    → intended write target
```

This is also why checking whether the checkpoint exists is insufficient. A manually written message can name a real existing checkpoint just as easily as a genuine squash message can.

There are 12 changed files:

- 5 production files: trailer parsing, commit hooks, attach, explain, and migration.
- 7 test files proving those behaviors.

We’ll take them one at a time.

## File 1: `trailers.go`

[trailers.go](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/fix-checkpoint-trailer-block/cmd/entire/cli/trailers/trailers.go:106) is the central commit-message parser.

Previously, Entire effectively had one checkpoint parser:

```go
ParseCheckpoint(message)
```

It searched the entire message:

```text
Subject

Entire-Checkpoint: A

More body text
```

Result:

```text
Found A
```

That behavior is necessary for finding checkpoint history, but unsafe for choosing where to write data.

The file now provides two kinds of parser.

### Discovery parser

The existing functions remain:

```go
ParseCheckpoint(message)
ParseAllCheckpoints(message)
```

They search the whole message.

Use them when asking:

> “Which checkpoints are mentioned in this commit?”

This preserves squash-merge history.

### Mutation parser

Two new functions were added:

```go
ParseCheckpointFromFinalTrailerBlock(message)
ParseAllCheckpointsFromFinalTrailerBlock(message)
```

They inspect only the final metadata section.

Use them when asking:

> “Which checkpoint did this commit officially designate?”

For example:

```text
Subject

Entire-Checkpoint: A

More body text

Signed-off-by: Muskan <muskan@example.com>
Entire-Checkpoint: B
```

The results are:

```text
Whole-message parser: A and B
Final-block parser:   B
```

So historical searching can find both, but a write operation may target only `B`.

### Trailer grammar was corrected

Indented text is not treated as a new trailer:

```text
  Entire-Checkpoint: A
```

But indentation is allowed as a continuation of a real trailer:

```text
Notes: This is a long note
 continued on another line
Entire-Checkpoint: B
```

The parser accepts the paragraph and finds only `B`.

`HasOPFApplied` was also moved onto the same strict final-block logic, so this body text no longer counts:

```text
  Entire-OPF-Applied: true
```

In simple terms, this file created the two rulebooks:

```text
Search rulebook → look everywhere
Write rulebook  → look only at official bottom metadata
```

Next file: `manual_commit_hooks.go`, where the commit lifecycle starts using the new write rulebook.
